{{short description|Generalized chain rule in calculus}}
{{Calculus |Differential}}
'''Faà di Bruno's formula''' is an identity in [[mathematics]] generalizing the [[chain rule]] to higher derivatives. It is named after {{harvs|txt|authorlink=Francesco Faà di Bruno|first=Francesco|last= Faà di Bruno|year=1855|year2=1857}}, although he was not the first to state or prove the formula. In 1800, more than 50 years before Faà di Bruno, the French mathematician [[Louis François Antoine Arbogast]] had stated the formula in a calculus textbook,<ref>{{harv|Arbogast|1800}}.</ref> which is considered to be the first published reference on the subject.<ref>According to {{harvtxt|Craik|2005|pp=120–122}}: see also the analysis of Arbogast's work by {{harvtxt|Johnson|2002|p=230}}.</ref>

Perhaps the most well-known form of Faà di Bruno's formula says that
{{Block indent|left=2|1={{Hanging indent
 |indent=10em
 |text=<math>{d^n \over dx^n} f(g(x)) = \sum \frac{n!}{m_1!\,1!^{m_1}\cdots m_n!\,n!^{m_n}} \cdot {}</math><math>f^{(m_1+\cdots+m_n)}(g(x)) \cdot {}</math><math>\prod_{j=1}^n \left(g^{(j)}(x)\right)^{m_j}</math>,
}}}}
where the sum is over all <math>n</math>-[[tuple]]s of nonnegative integers <math>(m_1,\ldots,m_n)</math> satisfying the constraint<math display="block">1\cdot m_1+2\cdot m_2+\cdots+n\cdot m_n=n.</math>Sometimes, to give it a memorable pattern, it is written in a way in which the coefficients that have the combinatorial interpretation discussed below are less explicit:

{{Block indent|left=2|1={{Hanging indent
 |indent=10em
 |text=<math>{d^n \over dx^n} f(g(x)) = \sum \frac{n!}{m_1!\,m_2!\,\cdots\,m_n!}\cdot {}</math><math>f^{(m_1+\cdots+m_n)}(g(x))\cdot {}</math><math>\prod_{j=1}^n\left(\frac{g^{(j)}(x)}{j!}\right)^{m_j}</math>.
}}}}

Combining the terms with the same value of <math>m_1+m_2+\cdots+m_n=k</math>
and noticing that <math>m_j</math> has to be zero for <math>j>n-k+1</math> leads to a somewhat simpler formula expressed in terms of partial (or incomplete) exponential [[Bell polynomials]] 
<math>B_{n,k}(x_1,\ldots,x_{n-k+1})</math>:

{{Block indent|left=2|1={{Hanging indent
 |indent=10em
 |text=<math>{d^n \over dx^n} f(g(x)) = \sum_{k=0}^n f^{(k)}(g(x))\cdot  {}</math><math>B_{n,k}\bigl(g'(x),g''(x),\dots,g^{(n-k+1)}(x)\bigr)</math>.
}}}}

This formula works for all <math>n \geq 0</math>, however for <math>n>0</math> the polynomials <math>B_{n,0}</math> are zero and thus summation in the formula can start with <math>k=1</math>.

== Combinatorial form ==

The formula has a "combinatorial" form:

<math display="block">{d^n \over dx^n} f(g(x))=(f\circ g)^{(n)}(x)=\sum_{\pi\in\Pi} f^{(\left|\pi\right|)}(g(x))\cdot\prod_{B\in\pi}g^{(\left|B\right|)}(x)</math>

where

* <math>\pi</math> runs through the set <math>\Pi</math> of all [[partition of a set|partitions of the set]] <math>\{1,\ldots,n\}</math>,
*"<math>B\in\pi</math>" means the variable <math>B</math> runs through the list of all of the "blocks" of the partition <math>\pi</math>, and
*<math>|A|</math> denotes the cardinality of the set <math>A</math> (so that <math>|\pi|</math> is the number of blocks in the partition <math>\pi</math> and <math>|B|</math> is the size of the block <math>B</math>).

==Example==
The following is a concrete explanation of the combinatorial form for the <math>n=4</math> case.

<math display="block">
\begin{align}
(f\circ g)''''(x)
= {} & f''''(g(x))g'(x)^4
+ 6f'''(g(x))g''(x)g'(x)^2 \\[8pt]
& {} +\; 3f''(g(x))g''(x)^2
+  4f''(g(x))g'''(x)g'(x) \\[8pt]
& {} +\; f'(g(x))g''''(x).
\end{align}
</math>

The pattern is:

<math display="block">
\begin{array}{cccccc}
  g'(x)^4 
& & \leftrightarrow & & 1+1+1+1 
& & \leftrightarrow & & f''''(g(x)) 
& & \leftrightarrow & & 1 
\\[12pt]
  g''(x)g'(x)^2 
& & \leftrightarrow & & 2+1+1 
& & \leftrightarrow & & f'''(g(x)) 
& & \leftrightarrow & & 6 
\\[12pt]
g''(x)^2 
& & \leftrightarrow & & 2+2 
& & \leftrightarrow & & f''(g(x)) 
& & \leftrightarrow & & 3 
\\[12pt]
g'''(x)g'(x) 
& & \leftrightarrow & & 3+1 
& & \leftrightarrow & & f''(g(x)) 
& & \leftrightarrow & & 4 
\\[12pt]
g''''(x) 
& & \leftrightarrow & & 4 
& & \leftrightarrow & & f'(g(x)) 
& & \leftrightarrow & & 1
\end{array}
</math>

The factor <math>g''(x)g'(x)^2 </math> corresponds to the partition 2 + 1 + 1 of the integer 4, in the obvious way.  The factor <math>f'''(g(x))</math> that goes with it corresponds to the fact that there are ''three'' summands in that partition.  The coefficient 6 that goes with those factors corresponds to the fact that there are exactly six partitions of a set of four members that break it into one part of size 2 and two parts of size 1.

Similarly, the factor <math>g''(x)^2 </math> in the third line corresponds to the partition 2 + 2 of the integer 4, (4, because we are finding the fourth derivative), while <math>f''(g(x)) </math> corresponds to the fact that there are ''two'' summands (2&nbsp;+&nbsp;2) in that partition. The coefficient 3 corresponds to the fact that there are <math>\tfrac{1}{2}\tbinom{4}{2}=3</math> ways of partitioning 4 objects into groups of&nbsp;2. The same concept applies to the others.

A memorizable scheme is as follows:

<math display="block">\begin{align} & \frac{D^1(f\circ{}g)}{1!} & = \left(f^{(1)}\circ{}g\right)\frac{\frac{g^{(1)} }{1!} }{1!} \\[8pt]
& \frac{D^2(f\circ g)}{2!} & = \left(f^{(1)}\circ{}g\right)\frac{\frac{g^{(2)} }{2!} }{1!} & {} + \left(f^{(2)}\circ{}g\right)\frac{\frac{g^{(1)} }{1!}\frac{g^{(1)} }{1!} }{2!} \\[8pt]
& \frac{D^3(f\circ g)}{3!} & = \left(f^{(1)}\circ{}g\right)\frac{\frac{g^{(3)} }{3!} }{1!} & {} + \left(f^{(2)}\circ{}g\right)\frac{\frac{g^{(1)} }{1!} }{1!}\frac{\frac{g^{(2)} }{2!} }{1!} & {} + \left(f^{(3)}\circ{}g\right)\frac{\frac{g^{(1)} }{1!}\frac{g^{(1)} }{1!}\frac{g^{(1)} }{1!} }{3!} \\[8pt]
& \frac{D^4(f\circ g)}{4!} & = \left(f^{(1)}\circ{}g\right)\frac{\frac{g^{(4)} }{4!} }{1!} & {} + \left(f^{(2)}\circ{}g\right)\left(\frac{\frac{g^{(1)} }{1!} }{1!}\frac{\frac{g^{(3)} }{3!} }{1!}+\frac{\frac{g^{(2)} }{2!}\frac{g^{(2)} }{2!} }{2!}\right) & {} + \left(f^{(3)}\circ{}g\right)\frac{\frac{g^{(1)} }{1!}\frac{g^{(1)} }{1!} }{2!}\frac{\frac{g^{(2)} }{2!} }{1!} & {} + \left(f^{(4)}\circ{}g\right)\frac{\frac{g^{(1)} }{1!}\frac{g^{(1)} }{1!}\frac{g^{(1)} }{1!}\frac{g^{(1)} }{1!} }{4!}
\end{align}</math>

==Variations==

===Multivariate version===

Let <math>y=g(x_1,\dots,x_n)</math>. Then the following identity holds regardless of whether the <math>n</math> variables are all distinct, or all identical, or partitioned into several distinguishable classes of indistinguishable variables (if it seems opaque, see the very concrete example below):<ref>{{cite journal |last=Hardy |first=Michael |title=Combinatorics of Partial Derivatives |journal=Electronic Journal of Combinatorics |volume=13 |issue=1 |year=2006 |pages=R1 |doi=10.37236/1027 |s2cid=478066 |url=http://www.combinatorics.org/Volume_13/Abstracts/v13i1r1.html|doi-access=free }}</ref>

<math display="block">{\partial^n \over \partial x_1 \cdots \partial x_n}f(y)
= \sum_{\pi\in\Pi} f^{(\left|\pi\right|)}(y)\cdot\prod_{B\in\pi}
{\partial^{\left|B\right|}y \over \prod_{j\in B} \partial x_j}</math>

where (as above)

* <math>\pi</math> runs through the set <math>\Pi</math> of all [[partition of a set|partitions of the set]] <math>\{1,\ldots,n\}</math>,
*"<math>B\in\pi</math>" means the variable <math>B</math> runs through the list of all of the "blocks" of the partition <math>\pi</math>, and
*<math>|A|</math> denotes the cardinality of the set <math>A</math> (so that <math>|\pi|</math> is the number of blocks in the partition <math>\pi</math> and 
<math>|B|</math> is the size of the block <math>B</math>).

More general versions hold for cases where the all functions are vector- and even [[Banach space|Banach-space-valued]]. In this case one needs to consider the [[Fréchet derivative]] or [[Gateaux derivative]].

; Example

The five terms in the following expression correspond in the obvious way to the five partitions of the set <math>\{1,2,3\}</math>, and in each case the order of the derivative of <math>f</math> is the number of parts in the partition:

<math display="block">
\begin{align}
{\partial^3 \over \partial x_1\, \partial x_2\, \partial x_3}f(y)
= {} & f'(y){\partial^3 y \over \partial x_1\, \partial x_2\, \partial x_3} \\[10pt]
& {} + f''(y) \left( {\partial y \over \partial x_1}
\cdot{\partial^2 y \over \partial x_2\, \partial x_3}
+{\partial y \over \partial x_2}
\cdot{\partial^2 y \over \partial x_1\, \partial x_3}
+ {\partial y \over \partial x_3}
\cdot{\partial^2 y \over \partial x_1\, \partial x_2}\right) \\[10pt]
& {} + f'''(y) {\partial y \over \partial x_1}
\cdot{\partial y \over \partial x_2}
\cdot{\partial y \over \partial x_3}.
\end{align}
</math>

If the three variables are indistinguishable from each other, then three of the five terms above are also indistinguishable from each other, and then we have the classic one-variable formula.

===Formal power series version===<!-- This section is linked from [[Formal power series]] -->
Suppose <math>f(x)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty {a_n} x^n</math> and <math>g(x)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty {b_n} x^n</math> are [[formal power series]] and <math>b_0 = 0</math>.

Then the composition <math>f \circ g</math> is again a formal [[power series]],
<math display="block">f(g(x))=\sum_{n=0}^\infty{c_n}x^n,</math>
where <math>c_0=a_0</math> and the other coefficient <math>c_n</math> for <math>n\geq 1</math> 
can be expressed as a sum over [[Composition (combinatorics)|compositions]] of <math>n</math> or as an equivalent sum over [[integer partition]]s of <math>n</math>:
<math display="block">c_{n} = \sum_{\mathbf{i}\in \mathcal{C}_{n}} a_{k} b_{i_{1}} b_{i_{2}} \cdots b_{i_{k}}, </math>
where 
<math display="block">\mathcal{C}_{n}=\{(i_1,i_2,\dots,i_k)\,:\ 1 \le k \le n,\ i_1+i_2+ \cdots + i_k=n\}</math>
is the set of compositions of <math>n</math> with <math>k</math> denoting the number of parts,

or
<math display="block">c_{n} = \sum_{k=1}^{n}  a_{k} \sum_{\mathbf{\pi}\in \mathcal{P}_{n,k}} \binom{k}{\pi_{1},\pi_{2}, \ldots, \pi_{n}} b_{1}^{\pi_{1}} b_{2}^{\pi_{2}}\cdots b_{n}^{\pi_{n}}, </math>
where
<math display="block">\mathcal{P}_{n,k}=\{(\pi_1,\pi_2,\dots,\pi_n)\,:\  \pi_1+\pi_2+ \cdots + \pi_n=k,\ \pi_{1}\cdot 1+\pi_{2}\cdot 2+ \cdots + \pi_{n}\cdot n = n \}</math>
is the set of partitions of <math>n</math> into <math>k</math> parts, in frequency-of-parts form.

The first form is obtained by picking out the  coefficient of <math>x^n</math>
in <math>(b_{1}x+b_{2}x^2+ \cdots)^{k} </math> "by inspection", and the second form
is then obtained by collecting like terms, or alternatively, by applying the [[multinomial theorem]].

The special case <math>f(x)=e^x</math>, <math>g(x)=\sum_{n\geq 1}\frac{1}{n!}a_n x^n</math> gives the [[exponential formula]].
The special case <math>f(x)=1/(1-x)</math>, <math>g(x)=\sum_{n\geq 1} (-a_n) x^n</math>
gives an expression for the [[Reciprocal (mathematics)|reciprocal]] of the formal power series 
<math>\sum_{n\geq 0} a_n x^n</math> in the case <math>a_0=1</math>.

Stanley<ref>See the "compositional formula" in Chapter 5 of {{cite book |last=Stanley |first=Richard P. |title=Enumerative Combinatorics |orig-year=1997 |year=1999 |isbn=978-0-521-55309-4|publisher=Cambridge University Press |url=http://www-math.mit.edu/~rstan/ec/}}</ref>
gives a version for exponential power series.
In the [[formal power series]]

<math display="block">f(x)=\sum_n {\frac{a_n}{n!}}x^n,</math>

we have the <math>n</math>th derivative at 0:

<math display="block">f^{(n)}(0)=a_n. </math>

This should not be construed as the value of a function, since these series are purely formal; there is no such thing as convergence or divergence in this context.

If

<math display="block">g(x)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty {\frac{b_n}{n!}} x^n</math>

and

<math display="block">f(x)=\sum_{n=1}^\infty {\frac{a_n}{n!}} x^n</math>

and

<math display="block">g(f(x))=h(x)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty{\frac{c_n}{n!}}x^n,</math>

then the coefficient <math>c_n</math> (which would be the <math>n</math>th derivative of <math>h</math> evaluated at 0 if we were dealing with convergent series rather than formal power series) is given by

<math display="block">c_n=\sum_{\pi=\left\{B_1,\ldots,B_k\right\}} a_{\left|B_1\right|}\cdots a_{\left|B_k\right|} b_k</math>

where <math>\pi</math> runs through the set of all partitions of the set <math>\{1,\ldots,n\}</math> and <math>B_1,\ldots,B_k</math>
are the blocks of the partition <math>\pi</math>, and <math>|B_j|</math>
is the number of members of the <math>j</math>th block, for <math>j=1,\ldots,k</math>.

This version of the formula is particularly well suited to the purposes of [[combinatorics]].

We can also write with respect to the notation above

<math display="block">g(f(x)) = b_0+ \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{\sum_{k=1}^n b_k B_{n,k}(a_1,\ldots,a_{n-k+1})}{n!} x^n,</math>

where <math>B_{n,k}(a_1,\ldots,a_{n-k+1})</math> are [[Bell polynomials]].

===A special case===

If <math>f(x) = e^x</math>, then all of the derivatives of <math>f</math> are the same and are a factor common to every term:  

<math display="block">{d^n \over dx^n} e^{g(x)} =  e^{g(x)} B_{n} \left(g'(x),g''(x), \dots, g^{(n)}(x)\right),</math>

where <math>B_n(x)</math> is the ''n''th [[Bell polynomials|complete exponential Bell polynomial]].

In case <math>g(x)</math> is a [[cumulant-generating function]], then <math>f(g(x))</math>
is a [[moment-generating function]], and the polynomial in various derivatives of <math>g</math> is the polynomial that expresses the [[moment (mathematics)|moment]]s as functions of the [[cumulant]]s.
